title: Weak After Diarrhoea, Blood Pressure Low / The Cause Is in the Drug History

blocks.text: Weak After Diarrhoea, Blood Pressure Low / The Cause Is in the Drug History

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-40 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 2) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: NICE NG148 Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management (published 18 December 2019; last updated 16 October 2024) · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: nephrectomy scar with a single kidney

Dear Doctor, a 74-year-old retired surveyor. Three days of vomiting and diarrhoea, now weak and dizzy. Known hypertension and osteoarthritis. Pulse 102, BP 98/58, temperature 37.1°C. Creatinine 214 µmol/L today (88 six months ago). Please assess and advise. He has consented to see you.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A rising creatinine after diarrhoea in a man on an ACE inhibitor and anti-inflammatories is acute kidney injury; the cause is in the drug history and the drugs stop today.

The Examiner Trap. He says it is a stomach bug and wants to go home to care for his wife. Candidates agree and leave his tablets unchanged. Pass: take a full drug history, stop the harmful drugs, offer admission. Fail: discharge on his usual drugs.

rows: He minimises it; start with his story.
"Tell me how this started, and what you're taking, including from the chemist."
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; open question; diarrhoea, fluids, urine, all medicines including over the counter.
Volume status and the effect of his drugs.
"May I check your blood pressure and examine you while you stay safely lying or seated?"
Supine or seated BP; assess perfusion and volume status, pulse, mucous membranes, JVP, chest, abdomen, bladder; stop if dizzy.
Name the cause and stop the harm.
"I think the diarrhoea and two of your tablets have strained your kidneys. Let's stop them."
Acute kidney injury; stop ibuprofen; hold the ACE inhibitor; blood tests; urine dipstick.
Share the options and the plan.
"I'd recommend a drip in hospital. With your low blood pressure and reduced urine, I recommend hospital assessment and monitored fluids today."
Benefits, risks, alternatives, doing nothing; arrange care for his wife; when to restart drugs.
Stands him up despite hypotension or dizziness; no consent
Introduces, obtains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, keeps him lying or seated and reassesses perfusion, covers him
Offers a chaperone, helps him sit if dizzy and thanks him
No drug history; stops at the diarrhoea
Asks fluids, urine, prescribed and over-the-counter medicines
Also asks how much ibuprofen he takes and what he does on a sick day
Ignores his wife and his fear
Acknowledges worry about his wife; asks what worries him
Finds the fear of dialysis and answers honestly
No blood pressure or volume check; reports pulmonary oedema that is absent
Supine or seated BP; assess perfusion and volume status, mucous membranes, abdomen; finds a hypotension and dry mouth
States negatives: chest clear, no oedema, no palpable bladder
Acute kidney injury from volume loss, an ACE inhibitor and an NSAID
Also considers obstruction, sepsis and nephritis, with reasons
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): continues his usual ACE inhibitor and ibuprofen, or sends him home with no blood tests
Urea and electrolytes, urine dipstick, stops NSAID, holds ACE inhibitor, fluids
Adds ECG and repeat potassium; urgent treatment if severe hyperkalaemia or ECG changes, avoids loop diuretics and routine ultrasound, asks a pharmacist
Clear recommendation for admission, benefits and risks; address barriers and informed refusal; checks understanding
Covers going home, doing nothing, care for his wife and when to restart drugs

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 74-year-old retired surveyor. Stoical, weak, a bit evasive. Carer for his wife.
Opening line. "It's a stomach bug. Give me something for the diarrhoea and I'll get home. My wife can't be left."
Volunteered. Three days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting after a takeaway. Dizzy when you stand and passing little urine.

Only if asked. You take ramipril and amlodipine for blood pressure (doses unknown), and buy ibuprofen from the chemist for your knees, about four times a day. Occasional paracetamol. No allergies. Gave up smoking thirty years ago; two pints at weekends; no travel. Your wife has dementia; your daughter lives thirty miles away. No blood in the diarrhoea.
Hidden concern. Your brother started dialysis last year and you are terrified of ending up the same. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it my kidneys?" "Will I need dialysis?" "Can I go home tonight?" "Who looks after my wife?" "Can I restart my tablets?"
How you react. Good handling: you relax, ask about your wife and agree to a drip once care is arranged. Poor handling: if told to stay without options you say "I'm going home".

Findings (released as each step is done). Pulse 102 regular; BP 98/58 while supine; no standing measurement is attempted; temperature 37.1°C; SpO2 97% (scenario values). Dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor. Chest clear; JVP not visible; no oedema. Abdomen soft, mildly tender, no guarding; bladder not palpable. Urine dipstick trace protein, no blood, nitrites or leucocytes. Urea 21 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L (scenario values).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis and cause (R5): acute kidney injury from volume loss, ACE inhibitor and NSAID. Q2 Tests (R6): urea and electrolytes, urine dipstick, ECG if potassium raised; ultrasound not routine when the cause is clear (NICE NG148 1.4.4). Q3 Treatment (R6): stop the NSAID, consider holding the ACE inhibitor (1.2.14), fluids, no routine loop diuretic (1.5.3). Q4 Restart (R7): when drinking and kidney function recover, per local protocol; avoid NSAIDs.
Curveball 1. "Give furosemide to make him pass urine." (R6) Safe: not routinely (NG148 1.5.3).
Curveball 2. "Scan his kidneys now." (R6) Safe: not routinely when the cause is identified.
Curveball 3. "I'm going home." (R7) Safe: he has capacity; explain risks, arrange care for his wife, agree a safety net.
Curveball 4. "Potassium is 6.5 with ECG changes." (R6) Safe: emergency treatment per local protocol.
Introduces, consents and asks about pain (G)
Asks about diarrhoea, fluids and urine output (C)
Asks about prescribed and over-the-counter medicines (C)
Acknowledges his worry about his wife and asks what worries him (F)
Measures blood pressure and perfusion while supine or seated and checks hydration (A)
Reports hypotension and dry mucous membranes (B)
Names acute kidney injury and links it to the drugs (D)
Requests tests, stops the NSAID and holds the ACE inhibitor (E)
Explains benefits, risks and alternatives of admission (E)
Summarises and checks understanding (C)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: What brings you in? [R1 Fail] (Does not ask about tablets. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Takes one blood pressure. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: It's gastroenteritis. [R5 Fail] Keep taking your tablets and drink fluids. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: You can go home. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No drug history, no adequate perfusion assessment, wrong diagnosis. Sending him home on his ACE inhibitor and ibuprofen is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): it risks worsening kidney injury.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. Is it all right to ask you some questions and examine you? Any pain? Please stay lying or seated while I assess your circulation. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: How much have you been drinking and passing? What do you take, including from the chemist? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Ramipril, amlodipine and ibuprofen for my knees. My wife can't be left.
CANDIDATE: Looking after your wife must be a worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Takes blood pressure and perfusion while supine or seated, checks mouth, chest and abdomen; covers him. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This is acute kidney injury from fluid loss, ramipril and ibuprofen. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'll check your kidney blood tests and urine, stop the ibuprofen, hold ramipril and give fluids. [R6 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I recommend a drip in hospital. With low blood pressure and reduced urine, I recommend admission and monitored treatment today; let us arrange support for your wife. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not find the fear of dialysis or plan care for his wife.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. Is it all right to ask you some questions and examine you? Any pain? Please stay lying or seated while I assess your circulation. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: How much have you been drinking and passing? What do you take, including from the chemist? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? Tell me if you feel dizzy and I'll help you sit. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: How many ibuprofen do you take a day, and what do you do about tablets on a sick day? [R2 High]
PATIENT: My brother is on dialysis. I'm frightened.

CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. Many people recover when the cause is treated, though I can't promise that; we'll watch your kidney tests closely and I'll tell you honestly if that changes. [R3 High]
(Takes blood pressure and perfusion while supine or seated, checks mouth, chest and abdomen; covers him. [R4 High])
(Notes chest clear, no oedema and no palpable bladder. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Kidney injury from dehydration and two drugs; obstruction, sepsis and nephritis are less likely. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll check your kidney blood tests and urine, stop the ibuprofen, hold ramipril and give fluids. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll check potassium and do an ECG if it is high; I'd avoid a diuretic and a routine scan. A pharmacist can review your tablets. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Staying lets us give fluids and watch your kidneys; going home risks worsening; doing nothing could be serious. We'll arrange care for your wife, and restart ramipril only when you've recovered, never ibuprofen. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Found the fear, avoided diuretic and scan, and tied the plan to his wife.
R6: Sending him home on his ACE inhibitor and ibuprofen is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): it risks worsening kidney injury.
R2: Not asking about over-the-counter medicines misses the NSAID that caused the injury.
R4: A single reading without repeated perfusion and volume assessment is inadequate; do not stand a hypotensive or dizzy patient.
R3: Ignoring his wife leaves the real barrier to admission unaddressed.
R7: Giving instructions without options leaves him without a say.
"What medicines do you take, even from the chemist?"
"I'd stop two of your tablets today."
"We can arrange care for your wife."

NICE NG148 (published 18 December 2019; last updated 16 October 2024): consider temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in adults with diarrhoea (1.2.14); do not routinely offer loop diuretics for acute kidney injury (1.5.3); do dipstick testing (1.4.2); no routine ultrasound when the cause is identified (1.4.4).
Over-the-counter anti-inflammatories raise the risk (NG148 1.6.4).
Seek pharmacist advice on medicines (1.2.13).

Treat as probable AKI with hypovolaemia and nephrotoxic contributors. The six-month-old creatinine is not enough to establish the NICE time-based AKI stage on its own: seek recent values and repeat testing. Admit, stop the NSAID, temporarily withhold ramipril (NG148 1.2.14: consider stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in adults with diarrhoea), hold amlodipine while he is hypotensive (clinical judgement; NG148 does not cover it), review other medicines and give isotonic IV fluid with frequent reassessment. Monitor urine output, creatinine, potassium and fluid balance; investigate obstruction or intrinsic disease if response or findings are atypical. Arrange a specific medicine restart and monitoring plan.
THINK: Hyperkalaemia; hypovolaemia.
SAY: "I think the diarrhoea and two of your tablets have strained your kidneys."
DO: Drug history; supine or seated BP and perfusion; stop drugs.
NUMBERS: Creatinine 214 µmol/L from 88; BP 98/58 supine (scenario values).
TRAP: Calling it gastroenteritis.
FINISH: Stop NSAID, hold ACE inhibitor, fluids, tests, plan for his wife.
